# Sinus node dysfunction

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Arrhythmias > Sinus node dysfunction*

[Original Article Link](/library/HS0Kaf)

---

## Summary

Sinus node dysfunction (SND), previously called sick sinus syndrome, is an abnormality in sinoatrial (SA) node <u>action potential</u> generation or conduction. It can be caused by factors intrinsic to the <u>SA node</u> (e.g., <u>fibrosis</u> of the <u>SA node</u>, infiltrative diseases) or extrinsic factors (e.g., pharmacotherapy with negative <u>chronotropes</u>, <u>hypothyroidism</u>) and most commonly results in <u>bradycardia</u>. Patients typically present with symptoms of end-organ <u>hypoperfusion</u> due to <u>bradycardia</u> (e.g., fatigue, <u>presyncope</u>, <u>syncope</u>, <u>dyspnea on exertion</u>). Establishing a temporal <u>correlation</u> between <u>symptoms of bradycardia</u> and <u>rhythm abnormalities of SND</u> (e.g., on <u>ECG</u>, <u>stress</u> testing, <u>cardiac monitoring</u>) confirms the diagnosis. <u>Unstable bradycardia</u> requires immediate implementation of <u>advanced cardiac life support</u> (<u>ACLS</u>) measures. <u>Reversible causes of SND</u> should be identified and managed. If reversible causes are not present, <u>permanent pacemaker</u> placement is preferred for long-term management of symptomatic patients. <u>Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome</u> is a subtype of SND that manifests as alternating episodes of <u>tachycardia</u> and <u>bradycardia</u> and is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events and mortality.




See also “<u>Management of bradycardia</u>” for related information.

---

## Etiology

### Intrinsic factors [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)




Conditions that alter the structure or function of the <u>SA node</u>




* Degeneration, <u>ischemia</u>, infiltration , or <u>fibrosis</u> of the <u>SA node</u> and surrounding <u>myocardium</u>

* Cardiac intervention (e.g., repair of a septal defect)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Idiopathic</u> degeneration of the <u>SA node</u> is the most common cause of SND. [[1]](/library/1M12nh0)[[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)




### Extrinsic factors [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




Factors external to the <u>SA node</u> that affect sinoatrial conduction




* Medications such as <u>β-blockers</u>, <u>digoxin</u>, and <u>nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers</u> (<u>verapamil</u>, <u>diltiazem</u>)

* Excessive <u>vagal</u> tone (e.g., athletes)

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities

* See “<u>Causes of bradycardia</u>” for details.





### Reversible causes of sinus node dysfunction [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




| <br>Potentially reversible or <u>treatable causes of sinus node dysfunction</u> [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Causes |
| Cardiac | <br><br>* <u>Acute myocardial infarction</u> or <u>ischemia</u><br><br>* Cardiac <u>surgery</u><br><br>* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u><br><br><br> |
| Metabolic | <br><br>* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>hyperkalemia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Hypoglycemia</u><br><br>* <u>Metabolic acidosis</u><br><br>* <u>Hypothermia</u><br><br>* <u>Hypothyroidism</u><br><br>* <u>Hypoxia</u><br><br>* <u>Hypercarbia</u><br><br><br> |
| Toxicity | <br><br>* Medications, such as:<br><br>* <u>Beta blockers</u><br><br>* <u>Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers</u><br><br>* <u>Digoxin</u><br><br>* <u>Antiarrhythmic drugs</u><br><br>* <u>Lithium</u><br><br>* <u>Methyldopa</u><br><br>* <u>Cisplatin</u><br><br>* <u>Risperidone</u><br><br>* <u>Recreational drug</u> use<br><br>* Toxins<br><br><br> |
| Increased <u>vagal</u> tone | <br><br>* <u>Reflex syncope</u><br><br>* Athletic <u>conditioning</u><br><br>* <u>Sleep apnea</u><br><br><br> |
| Other | <br><br>* Infections, such as:<br><br>* <u>Lyme disease</u><br><br>* <u>Typhoid fever</u><br><br>* <u>Typhus</u><br><br>* <u>Malaria</u><br><br>* <u>Dengue fever</u><br><br>* <u>Leptospirosis</u><br><br>* <u>Hypovolemic shock</u><br><br><br> |

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Symptoms of bradycardia</u> (features of end-organ <u>hypoperfusion</u>) [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)

* Fatigue

* <u>Dizziness</u> or <u>lightheadedness</u>, <u>syncope</u>, <u>presyncope</u>, <u>TIA</u> (seen in ∼ 50% of patients) [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)

* Decreased physical activity tolerance

* <u>Stokes-Adams attacks</u>

* <u>Dyspnea on exertion</u>

* <u>Angina</u>, <u>palpitations</u>

* <u>Oliguria</u>

* Patients with <u>tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome</u> will also present with <u>symptoms of tachycardia</u>, including <u>palpitations</u>.





> [!TIP]
> The identification of a temporal <u>correlation</u> between <u>symptoms of bradycardia</u> and <u>rhythm abnormalities of SND</u> is considered the <u>gold standard</u> for diagnosing SND. In some individuals, SND may be asymptomatic in the early stages; symptomatic patients have a higher risk of cardiovascular events. [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Correlate symptoms with <u>rhythm abnormalities of SND</u>. 

* Obtain 12-lead <u>ECG</u>.

* Inconclusive <u>ECG</u> findings: Perform <u>ambulatory cardiac monitoring</u>.

* Symptoms on exertion: Perform <u>exercise stress test</u>.

* Evaluate for an underlying cause.

* Evaluate all patients for <u>reversible causes of SND</u>: including <u>medication review</u>, <u>BMP</u>, <u>HbA1c</u>, <u>thyroid function tests</u>

* Obtain additional studies (e.g., nocturnal <u>polysomnography</u>, <u>TTE</u>) as needed. [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)[[4]](/library/jdb_ps)

* Refer for specialist evaluation for alternative diagnoses or advanced diagnostics if symptoms do not correlate with rhythm abnormalities.





> [!WARNING]
> In <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> patients, start immediate treatment for <u>unstable bradycardia</u> without waiting for diagnostic confirmation.




### <u>ECG</u> studies [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Preferred initial diagnostic study: 12-lead <u>ECG</u>

* Second line : <u>ambulatory cardiac monitoring</u> (typically in the following order)

* <u>Holter monitor</u> or <u>external patch recorder</u>

* <u>Event monitor</u> or <u>mobile cardiovascular telemetry</u>

* <u>External patch recorder</u> or <u>implantable loop recorder</u>

* Supportive findings: The presence of any of the following <u>rhythm abnormalities of SND</u> with accompanying symptoms of end-organ <u>hypoperfusion</u> is diagnostic of SND. [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)





| <br>Rhythm abnormalities of SND [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Bradycardia</u> | <br>* <u>Heart rate</u> < 50 bpm<br><br>* <u>Sinus rhythm</u>: <u>sinus bradycardia</u><br><br>* <u>Ectopic</u> rhythm: <u>ectopic atrial bradycardia</u> (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation</u> with slow ventricular rate) [[5]](/library/nCY7sr)[[6]](/library/3DYSVr)<br><br> |
| Inappropriate or absent impulse generation by the <u>SA node</u> pacemaker cells | <br><br>* Sinus arrest: temporary absence of <u>SA node</u> <u>depolarization</u> (absent <u>P waves</u>)<br><br>* Sinus pause: <u>SA node</u> <u>depolarization</u> > 3 seconds after the preceding atrial <u>depolarization</u><br><br>* <u>Sinus arrest</u> or pause may be followed by an <u>escape rhythm</u><br><br><br> |
| Inappropriate impulse transmission by the <u>SA node</u> transitional cells | <br><br>* Sinoatrial exit block: impaired conduction between <u>SA node</u> and adjacent atrial tissue (e.g., intermittent dropped <u>P wave</u>)<br><br>* Isorhythmic dissociation: <u>atria</u> <u>depolarization</u> slower than ventricular <u>depolarization</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome</u> | <br>* <u>Bradycardia</u> alternating with intermittent atrial <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>  [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)[[7]](/library/5JciuW0)<br><br> |
| <br><u>Chronotropic incompetence</u> [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)<br> | <br>* <u>Heart rate</u> does not increase sufficiently in response to increased activity or demand. <br><br>* Seen in up to 50% of patients with SND [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)<br><br>* Identified on <u>exercise stress testing</u><br><br> |

### Evaluation for an underlying cause [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




Evaluate all patients for common <u>reversible causes of SND</u> as clinically indicated (i.e., based on history and <u>physical examination</u>). [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>BMP</u> with <u>magnesium</u>

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>

* <u>Hemoglobin A1C</u>

* Consider <u>genetic testing</u> (e.g., for SCN5A, HCN4 mutations) in consultation with a specialist.  [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)





#### Additional studies [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)[[4]](/library/jdb_ps)




* <u>Sleep</u>-related symptoms: Consider nocturnal <u>polysomnography</u>.

* Concern for <u>structural heart disease</u> : <u>transthoracic echocardiogram</u> (<u>TTE</u>)

* Suspected structural and/or infiltrative <u>heart</u> disease that cannot be confirmed with other diagnostic techniques: Consider advanced imaging





### Advanced diagnostics [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)[[4]](/library/jdb_ps)




* Indications: diagnostic uncertainty in symptomatic patients

* Modalities

* <u>Electrophysiology studies</u>: may show prolonged sinus node recovery time in SND

* Oral <u>theophylline</u> challenge test: Consider prior to pacemaker insertion if a documented <u>bradyarrhythmia</u> and symptoms are both present but the <u>correlation</u> is uncertain





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Electrophysiology studies</u> are not recommended in asymptomatic patients, as it is an invasive modality and the risks outweigh the potential benefits. [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)

---

## Treatment

The long-term management of SND is detailed here. See “<u>Management of unstable bradycardia</u>” for initial management of SND causing hemodynamic compromise or severe symptoms.




### General principles [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Asymptomatic patients: observation

* Symptomatic patients

* Manage <u>reversible causes of SND</u>.

* Severe and/or frequent <u>symptoms of bradycardia</u> due to irreversible causes

* First-line (after patient stabilization): <u>permanent pacemaker</u> placement

* Alternative: <u>phosphodiesterase inhibitors</u>

* <u>Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome</u>: See “Subtypes and variants” for details.





> [!TIP]
> Permanent pacing should not be performed based on <u>ECG</u> findings alone. Permanent pacing is not recommended for asymptomatic patients. [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




> [!TIP]
> Oral anticoagulation is not routinely recommended for patients with SND unless another indication for anticoagulation is present. [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)




### Management of the underlying cause [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Indication: first-line management of patients with <u>reversible causes of SND</u>

* Examples

* Stop or decrease the dosage of nonessential medications; see “<u>Medication-induced bradycardia</u>” for management of drug toxicity.

* <u>Management of hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>Management of obstructive sleep apnea</u>





### <u>Permanent pacemaker</u> placement [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)[[4]](/library/jdb_ps)




Permanent pacing decreases symptom frequency and improves quality of life.  [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Indications

* First-line management for symptomatic SND  caused by intrinsic or irreversible extrinsic factors

* Symptomatic SND caused by essential medications that cannot be stopped

* Symptomatic SND with <u>chronotropic incompetence</u>

* Important considerations: Permanent pacing is not routinely recommended in the following circumstances [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)

* Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic SND

* Symptoms in the absence of <u>rhythm abnormalities of SND</u>

* Nocturnal SND





> [!TIP]
> Establishing a temporal <u>correlation</u> between symptoms and rhythm abnormalities aids patient selection for permanent pacing, as permanent pacing is most effective in these patients. [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)[[4]](/library/jdb_ps)




> [!WARNING]
> Rule out <u>reversible causes of SND</u> before considering <u>permanent pacemaker</u> placement. [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




### <u>Phosphodiesterase inhibitors</u> [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Indication: second-line option for patients in whom permanent pacing is indicated but cannot be performed

* Agents: <u>theophylline</u>, <u>cilostazol</u>

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome




#### Definition [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* A subtype of SND in which there are alternating periods of <u>bradyarrhythmia</u> and atrial <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> (typically <u>atrial fibrillation</u>)

* Present in 40–50% of patients with SND [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[8]](/library/cDcaWe0)

* Associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)





#### Clinical features [[2]](/library/1Dc2We0)[[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Symptoms vary in intensity depending on the extent of <u>bradycardia</u> and <u>tachycardia</u>.

* <u>Symptoms of bradycardia</u> and <u>symptoms of tachycardia</u>, e.g.:

* Recurrent <u>syncope</u> or <u>presyncope</u>

* <u>Palpitations</u>

* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* <u>Angina pectoris</u>

* Symptoms of atrial <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>-associated thromboembolic complications, e.g., <u>stroke</u>.





#### Diagnostics




* Diagnostic studies and findings are similar to those for SND.

* Rhythm abnormalities: alternating atrial <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation</u> , <u>atrial tachycardia</u> , <u>atrial flutter</u> ) and <u>bradycardia</u> (e.g., <u>sinus bradycardia</u>, <u>ectopic atrial bradycardia</u>, <u>sinus pause</u>)   [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)[[4]](/library/jdb_ps)[[7]](/library/5JciuW0)





![Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome](media/tqyej5hf5wtl45r8cq7z5nq1.jpg)

Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome




#### Treatment [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




##### <u>Arrhythmia</u> control




* <u>Bradycardia</u> not triggered by atrial <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>

* <u>Permanent pacemaker</u> placement

* Followed by  treatment for <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> 

* e.g., β1-selective <u>beta blockers</u> (<u>cardioselective beta blockers</u>)

* See “Treatment of <u>atrial fibrillation</u>.”

* <u>Bradycardia</u> triggered by atrial <u>tachyarrhythmia</u> 

* Consider <u>ablation</u> as the sole treatment.

* If <u>ablation</u> is unsuitable or unsuccessful, treat with a pacemaker and <u>rate control</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Pharmacotherapy for <u>tachyarrhythmia</u> can trigger <u>complete heart block</u>, <u>asystole</u>, and <u>bradyarrhythmias</u> in patients without a pacemaker. [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Ablation</u> for atrial <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> may be sufficient for the management of both <u>tachycardia</u> and <u>bradycardia</u> in patients with <u>tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome</u>. [[3]](/library/ntY7VI)




##### <u>Thromboembolism</u> prophylaxis




* Patients are at an increased risk of cardiovascular events.

* Assess the need for anticoagulation based on patient <u>risk factors</u> and type of <u>tachyarrhythmia</u> (e.g., see “<u>Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation</u>.”)
